claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 exhibits a hierarchical heterostructure spanning nanoscale precipitates and microscale grain/interphase arrangements.
High-resolution SEM/TEM can provide detailed descriptors of nanoscale precipitates, grain-boundary distributions, and secondary-phase networks in this alloy.
A hierarchical bridging strategy can capture local stress transfer across the HfNbTiVAl10 heterostructure.
Nanoscale precipitates and grain-boundary distributions mediate local stress concentrations in the hierarchical heterostructure.
Nanoscale precipitates and grain-boundary distributions mediate deformation mechanisms in the hierarchical heterostructure.
Multiscale descriptors in the machine-learning model can quantitatively capture the effects of the heterostructure on local stress and deformation.
Directly linking microstructural features to macroscopic mechanical responses allows the machine-learning protocol to bypass computationally expensive full-field simulations.
The proposed approach enhances phase-space overlap between local deformation modes and global mechanical responses.
Conventional homogenized simulations have thermodynamic-integration path mismatches that the proposed approach reduces.
The machine-learning-enhanced simulation will predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture-initiation thresholds at least 10% more accurately than established simulations.
The machine-learning-enhanced simulation will reduce computational time by approximately a factor of two relative to established simulations.
The approach is applicable to quasi-static tensile and fracture loading at ambient temperature.
High-strain-rate or dynamic loading may cause the approach to fail.
Environmental effects that induce phase changes and alter the hierarchical structure may cause the approach to fail.
Descriptor selection and scaling may affect model performance and transferability across different heterostructural configurations.

The hypothesis is rejected if the model fails to improve prediction accuracy by at least 10%, fails to reduce runtime by roughly a factor of two, or produces errors exceeding 10% relative to independent measurements.
